solution: Elasticity is the property by virtue of which a body regains its original shape and size after the deforming force acting on it is removed.
Deformation is the change in shape or size, or both, of a body produced by an external (deforming) force.
The SI unit of stress is \(\text{N m}^{-2}\) (pascal, Pa) and its dimensions are \([L^{-1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\).
Strain is the ratio of the change in the dimensions of a body to its original dimensions; being a ratio of two similar quantities it is dimensionless and has no unit.

For a perfectly rigid body the change in length is zero, so the longitudinal strain is zero and \(Y = \dfrac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}\) becomes infinite.

[Note: the chapter defines \(Y\) by Eq. (6.12) and says it measures a solid's resistance to elongation, but it does not itself discuss the rigid-body case; the answer above follows directly from that definition with strain \(= 0\).]

[Textbook note: the expected answer is elastic fatigue, but this chapter never develops the idea — the words "bridge" and "fatigue" appear nowhere in its fourteen pages except inside this question. The answer above gives the elastic-fatigue explanation AND says the term is imported, pointing instead at the mechanism the chapter does supply: the permanent set beyond the yield point in §6.6, elastic hysteresis, and the loop area as energy dissipated per cycle.]

Over years of use a bridge is loaded and unloaded again and again, and repeated stressing gradually leaves it with a permanent set, so that its elastic properties are reduced and it can fail at a load it once carried safely. This gradual loss of elasticity under repeated stress is called elastic fatigue.

[Note: the words "bridge" and "fatigue" do not appear anywhere in this chapter, so the term is being brought in from outside it. What the chapter does supply is the mechanism: section 6.6 shows that once a wire is taken beyond the yield point B and the load is removed it follows the line CE and "has acquired a permanent set", and it describes elastic hysteresis, where the strain lags behind the stress and the area of the loop is the energy dissipated in each cycle. The p-07 "Can you tell?" box asks the same question in miniature: why does a rubber band become loose after repeated use?]

The force must be applied tangentially, that is parallel to the surface of the body (parallel to the top and bottom faces of the block) while the opposite face is held fixed, so that the shape changes without any change in size.
Hooke's law holds good only within the elastic limit, that is up to the proportional limit of the material, where the deformation is small and the stress is directly proportional to the strain.

Within the elastic limit, Poisson's ratio \(\sigma\) is the ratio of the lateral strain to the linear (longitudinal) strain, \(\sigma = \dfrac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{linear strain}}\); it is a pure number with no unit and no dimensions.
An elastomer is a material such as rubber that can be stretched elastically to a very large value of strain, its stress-strain curve not being a straight line.

Elastic hysteresis is the lagging of strain behind stress, seen in materials such as vulcanized rubber, where the strain does not return to zero immediately when the stress applied on the body is reduced to zero; the loop enclosed by the loading and unloading curves has an area equal to the energy dissipated during the deformation.

Diamond is the hardest material, and among the materials this chapter names, aluminium is the softest (section 6.8 gives diamond as the best known hard material and calls aluminium the metal of very low hardness).

[Note: the chapter names aluminium only as the metal of very low hardness; it does not name a softest material outright. On the Mohs scale the softest common mineral is talc, but that is outside this chapter.]
Friction is the property which resists the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.

Because the force of static friction automatically increases to become equal and opposite to the applied force, keeping the body at rest, until the applied force reaches the limiting value; and if the direction of the applied force is reversed the direction of static friction reverses too, so it adjusts both its magnitude and its direction.

The coefficient of friction depends on (a) the materials of the two surfaces in contact and (b) the nature of those surfaces, that is how rough or smooth they are.

This is the third law of static friction in section 6.9.2, which states that the limiting force of friction depends upon the materials in contact and the nature of their surfaces; Table 6.4 shows the effect directly, since \(\mu_s\) is \(0.4\) for Teflon on Teflon and \(1.0\) for rubber on dry concrete.

| Elasticity | Plasticity |
|---|---|
| The body regains its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed. | The body does not regain its original shape and size; it retains the altered shape or size after the deforming force is removed. |
| The restoring forces are strong enough to bring the displaced molecules back to their original positions. | The restoring forces are not strong enough to bring the molecules back to their original positions. |
| A body showing this property is called an elastic body; if it recovers completely and instantaneously it is perfectly elastic. | A body showing this property is called a plastic body. |
| Examples: metals, rubber, quartz. | Examples: clay, putty, plasticine, thick mud. |

No solid is perfectly elastic or perfectly plastic; the nearest to an ideal elastic solid is quartz fibre and the nearest to a plastic body is putty.

[Textbook note: the question asks for four methods of reducing friction, and the chapter's own list supplies two. The answer above completes them from §6.9 (polishing) and the chapter's rolling-versus-sliding comparison. Note also that §6.9.1 states that extreme polishing INCREASES friction, which the chapter never reconciles with the advice in §6.9.]

Four methods of reducing friction:

1. Polishing the surfaces in contact, so that the irregularities which interlock are removed.
2. Using lubricants such as oil or grease between the moving parts of a machine.
3. Using ball bearings, which convert kinetic friction into rolling friction.
4. Making a body roll rather than slide (using wheels or rollers), since for the same pair of surfaces rolling friction is the smallest of the three types.

[Note: the chapter's own bulleted list under "Methods of reducing friction" gives only the first two of the four above; polishing comes from section 6.9 and rolling from the comparison of the three types of friction in section 6.9.2. Note also the caution in section 6.9.1, that if the surfaces are made extremely smooth the actual area of contact increases and the friction may then increase rather than decrease, so polishing helps only up to a point.]

Friction between two bodies in contact when one body is rolling over the other is called rolling friction. Motion is said to be rolling when the point of contact of the body with the surface keeps changing continuously.

How it arises: friction of any kind arises from the force of attraction between the molecules of the two surfaces that are in actual contact, together with the interlocking of the irregularities on those surfaces (section 6.9.1). In rolling, the point of contact does not stay put, so these bonds and interlockings are made and broken continuously over a very small region instead of being dragged along the surface. This is why rolling friction is smaller than both static and kinetic friction, and why ball bearings are used to reduce friction in machine parts.

[Note: the chapter states the general origin of friction and states that rolling friction is the least of the three, but it does not set out a separate mechanism for rolling friction; the middle paragraph applies the chapter's general account to the rolling case.]

Friction is caused by the force of attraction between the molecules of the two surfaces that are in actual contact, together with the interlocking of their irregularities. A lubricant such as oil or grease is a different material introduced between the two surfaces. It fills up the irregularities and keeps the two solid surfaces apart, so that they are no longer in direct contact over their tiny high-pressure contact points. The strong cohesive or adhesive attraction between the two solids is therefore replaced by the much weaker resistance of a thin fluid layer, and the friction is reduced. This is why lubricants are used in the moving parts of machines, where friction would otherwise dissipate energy and lower the efficiency of the machine.

Laws of static friction:

1. The limiting force of static friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction \(N\) between the two surfaces in contact: \(F_L \propto N\), so \(F_L = \mu_s N\), where \(\mu_s\) is the coefficient of static friction.
2. The limiting force of friction is independent of the apparent area between the surfaces in contact, so long as the normal reaction remains the same.
3. The limiting force of friction depends upon the materials in contact and the nature of their surfaces.

Laws of kinetic friction:

1. The force of kinetic friction \(F_k\) is directly proportional to the normal reaction between the two surfaces in contact: \(F_k \propto N\), so \(F_k = \mu_k N\), where \(\mu_k\) is the coefficient of kinetic friction.
2. The force of kinetic friction is independent of the shape and the apparent area of the surfaces in contact.
3. The force of kinetic friction depends upon the nature and material of the surfaces in contact.
4. The magnitude of the force of kinetic friction is independent of the relative velocity between the object and the surface, provided that the relative velocity is neither too large nor too small.

Advantages of friction:

1. We can walk because of the friction between the ground and our feet.
2. We can hold an object in the hand because of static friction.
3. The brakes of vehicles work because of friction, so we can slow down or stop a vehicle.
4. Climbing a tree is possible because of friction.

Disadvantages of friction:

1. Friction opposes motion.
2. Friction produces heat in the different parts of a machine, and it also produces noise.
3. Automobile engines consume more fuel because of friction.

More generally, friction causes a dissipation of energy in machines, which lowers their efficiency.

A brittle substance is one that breaks while it is still within the elastic limit, that is it fractures without showing any appreciable plastic deformation first. Two examples are glass and ceramics.

On the stress-strain curve of section 6.6, a brittle material fractures in the straight-line elastic region OA to B, whereas a ductile material such as copper or wrought iron has a long plastic range from B to D and lengthens considerably before it breaks.

There are three types of stress and strain, and hence three moduli of elasticity, one for each.

| Point of difference | Young's modulus \(Y\) | Bulk modulus \(K\) | Modulus of rigidity \(\eta\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| What changes | Length of the body | Volume of the body | Shape of the body |
| Type of stress | Longitudinal (tensile or compressive) stress; force normal to the cross section, applied along the length | Volume or hydraulic stress; force normal and uniform over the entire surface | Shearing or tangential stress; force parallel to the surface |
| Definition | \(Y = \dfrac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}}\) | \(K = \dfrac{\text{volume stress}}{\text{volume strain}}\) | \(\eta = \dfrac{\text{shear stress}}{\text{shear strain}}\) |
| Formula | \(Y = \dfrac{MgL}{\pi r^{2} l}\) | \(K = -\,\dfrac{V\,dP}{dV}\) | \(\eta = \dfrac{F/A}{\theta}\) |
| Also called | Elasticity of length | Elasticity of volume | Rigidity modulus |
| Shown by | Solids only | Solids, liquids and gases | Solids only, since they alone have a definite shape |
| What it indicates | Resistance to elongation or compression | Resistance offered while an attempt is made to change the volume | Resistance offered to a change of shape |

All three have the SI unit \(\text{N m}^{-2}\) and the dimensions \([L^{-1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\).

**Stress.** When a body is deformed by an applied force, restoring forces are set up inside it which oppose the change in its shape or size. When the body is in equilibrium in its altered shape or size, the deforming force and the restoring force are equal and opposite. The internal restoring force per unit area of the body is called stress:

\[ \text{stress} = \frac{F}{A} \]

Its SI unit is \(\text{N m}^{-2}\) (pascal) and its dimensions are \([L^{-1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\).

**Strain.** Strain is a measure of the deformation of a body. It is defined as the ratio of the change in the dimensions of the body to its original dimensions:

\[ \text{strain} = \frac{\text{change in dimension}}{\text{original dimension}} \]

Being the ratio of two similar quantities it is dimensionless and has no unit.

**Types.** There are three types of stress and three corresponding strains.

1. **Tensile (longitudinal) stress and tensile strain.** A force applied along the length of a body, perpendicular to its cross section \(A\), elongates it; the restoring force per unit area is the tensile stress, \(\dfrac{|\vec{F}|}{A}\). If the rod is instead pushed at its two ends by equal and opposite forces its length decreases and the restoring force per unit area is called compressive stress. The strain produced is the tensile or linear strain, \(\dfrac{\Delta l}{L}\), where \(L\) is the original length and \(\Delta l\) the change in length.
2. **Volume (hydraulic) stress and volume strain.** A force acting normally and uniformly all over the surface area \(A\) of a body changes its size without changing its shape; the restoring force per unit area is the volume or hydraulic stress. The strain produced is the volume strain, \(\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}\), where \(V\) is the original volume.
3. **Shearing (tangential) stress and shearing strain.** A tangential force acting on a surface of area \(A\), parallel to the top and bottom faces of a block whose opposite face is fixed, changes the shape of the body without changing its size; the restoring force per unit area is the shearing or tangential stress. The top face is displaced relative to the bottom face by a small distance \(\Delta l\), and the shearing strain is \(\dfrac{\Delta l}{l} = \tan\theta \approx \theta\) for small \(\Delta l\), where \(\theta\) is measured in radian.

**Young's modulus.** Young's modulus \(Y\) is the modulus of elasticity related to the change in length of an object such as a wire, rod or beam under an applied deforming force, and it is defined as the ratio of the longitudinal stress to the longitudinal strain within the elastic limit:

\[ Y = \frac{\text{longitudinal stress}}{\text{longitudinal strain}} \]

It is also called the elasticity of length, its SI unit is \(\text{N m}^{-2}\) and its dimensions are \([L^{-1}M^{1}T^{-2}]\). It is a property of solids only.

**Experiment to find \(Y\) for a long straight wire.**

1. Take a long, thin, uniform wire of the given material and suspend it vertically from a rigid support.
2. Measure its original length \(L\) from the point of support to the free end, and measure its radius \(r\) at several places along its length with a screw gauge, taking the mean value. The cross-sectional area is then \(A = \pi r^{2}\).
3. Attach a load of mass \(M\) to the free end. The deforming force acting at the free end, in the downward direction, is \(F = Mg\), so

\[ \text{longitudinal stress} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{Mg}{\pi r^{2}} \]

4. The wire stretches. If the new length is \(L + l\), then \(l\) is the extension or elongation of the wire. Measure \(l\) with a suitable arrangement that can read a very small displacement, such as a vernier scale or a travelling microscope focused on a reference mark at the lower end of the wire. Then

\[ \text{longitudinal strain} = \frac{l}{L} \]

5. Repeat for several loads, keeping every load within the elastic limit of the wire, and take the mean.
6. Young's modulus of the material is then

\[ Y = \frac{Mg/\pi r^{2}}{l/L} = \frac{MgL}{\pi r^{2} l} \]

**Precautions.** The wire must be long and thin so that the extension is measurable, it must be free of kinks, the loads must be added gently and kept within the elastic limit, and the length and radius must be measured accurately, since \(r\) enters the result as \(r^{2}\).

[Note: the arrangement, the symbols and the final formula are the chapter's own (section 6.5.1, Eq. 6.10 to 6.13). The chapter does not prescribe an instrument for measuring \(l\), nor does it list precautions; step 4 and the precautions are the standard laboratory practice for this measurement.]

Consider a wire of original length \(L\) and cross-sectional area \(A\), stretched by a force \(F\) acting along its length so that an elongation \(l\) is produced. Within the elastic limit the stress and the strain increase in proportion, and

\[ Y = \frac{F/A}{l/L} = \frac{FL}{Al} \qquad \therefore\; F = \frac{Y A l}{L} \]

The stretching force does not act at its full value throughout: it increases from zero to \(F\) as the wire elongates. Let \(f\) be the force at the stage where the extension is \(x\). Then

\[ f = \frac{Y A x}{L} \]

For a further extension \(dx\), the work done is

\[ dW = f\,dx = \frac{YAx}{L}\,dx \]

The total work done in stretching the wire from \(x = 0\) to \(x = l\) is

\[ W = \int_{0}^{l} \frac{YAx}{L}\,dx = \frac{YA}{L}\int_{0}^{l} x\,dx = \frac{YA}{L}\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{l} = \frac{YAl^{2}}{2L} \]

Writing \(\dfrac{YAl}{L} = F\), this becomes

\[ W = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{YAl}{L}\,l = \frac{1}{2}Fl = \frac{1}{2}\,(\text{load})\,(\text{extension}) \]

This work done by the stretching force is stored in the wire as elastic potential energy, and it is called the strain energy.

**Strain energy per unit volume.** The volume of the wire is \(AL\), so

\[ \text{strain energy per unit volume} = \frac{W}{AL} = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}Fl}{AL} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{F}{A}\right)\left(\frac{l}{L}\right) \]

\[ \therefore\; \text{strain energy per unit volume} = \frac{1}{2}\,(\text{stress})\,(\text{strain}) \]

Since \(Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}\), we may write \(\text{stress} = Y\,(\text{strain})\) or \(\text{strain} = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{Y}\), which gives two further forms of the same result:

\[ \text{strain energy per unit volume} = \frac{1}{2}\,Y\,(\text{strain})^{2} = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{(\text{stress})^{2}}{Y} \]

The SI unit of strain energy per unit volume is \(\text{J m}^{-3}\).

**Friction.** Whenever the surface of one body slides over another, each body exerts a force on the other which is tangential to the surfaces and opposite to the direction of relative motion between them. This mechanical force between two solid surfaces in contact is called the frictional force, and the property which resists the relative motion between two surfaces in contact is called friction.

**Coefficient of static friction.** The frictional force which balances the applied force while the body is still static is called the force of static friction. It is self adjusting: as the applied force is increased the friction increases with it, until just before the body starts to slide it reaches its maximum value, called the limiting force of friction \(F_L\). By the first law of static friction, \(F_L\) is directly proportional to the normal reaction \(N\) between the two surfaces:

\[ F_L \propto N \qquad \therefore\; F_L = \mu_s N \qquad \therefore\; \mu_s = \frac{F_L}{N} \]

The coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s\) is thus defined as the ratio of the limiting force of friction to the normal reaction. For a body of mass \(m\) resting on a horizontal surface, \(N = mg\), so the least force needed to just start the motion is \(F_L = \mu_s mg\).

**Coefficient of kinetic friction.** Once sliding has begun the force of friction decreases, so the force needed to keep a body sliding steadily is less than the force needed to just start it sliding. The friction that comes into play when a body is in a steady state of motion over another surface is called the force of kinetic (or dynamic) friction, \(F_k\). By the first law of kinetic friction it too is directly proportional to the normal reaction:

\[ F_k \propto N \qquad \therefore\; F_k = \mu_k N \qquad \therefore\; \mu_k = \frac{F_k}{N} \]

The coefficient of kinetic friction \(\mu_k\) is thus defined as the ratio of the force of kinetic friction to the normal reaction between the two surfaces in contact.

Both \(\mu_s\) and \(\mu_k\) are pure numbers with no unit and no dimensions. For the same pair of surfaces \(\mu_s > \mu_k\); comparing Tables 6.4 and 6.5, steel on steel has \(\mu_s = 0.74\) against \(\mu_k = 0.57\).

**Hooke's law.** Within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain.

\[ \text{stress} \propto \text{strain} \qquad \therefore\; \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} = \text{constant} \]

The constant is called the modulus of elasticity of the material. It is the slope of the stress-strain curve in the elastic region and depends on the nature of the material. The maximum value of stress up to which stress remains directly proportional to strain is called the elastic limit.

**The graph.** Suspend a metal wire vertically from a rigid support and stretch it by loading its lower end, increasing the load gradually in small steps until the wire breaks, measuring the elongation at each step. Plot tensile strain along the x-axis and tensile stress along the y-axis. The curve obtained has the following parts:

| Part of the curve | What happens there |
|---|---|
| \(OA\), a straight line through the origin | Stress is directly proportional to strain. **This is the region in which Hooke's law is obeyed.** The stress at \(A\) is called the proportional limit. |
| \(A\) to \(B\) | Stress and strain are no longer proportional, so Hooke's law is not valid; but if the load is removed anywhere between \(O\) and \(B\) the curve is retraced and the wire regains its original length, so the material is still elastic over \(OB\). \(B\) is the yield point and the corresponding point is the elastic limit. |
| \(B\) to \(C\) to \(D\) | Beyond \(B\) the strain keeps increasing. If the load is removed at a point such as \(C\), the material follows the line \(CE\) and does not regain its original length: it has acquired a permanent set. This is the region of plastic flow or plastic deformation, and the change is irreversible. |
| At \(D\) | A large increase in strain occurs for a relatively small increase in stress, and fracture takes place. \(D\) is the breaking point. |

So on the labelled graph the axes are tensile strain (x-axis) against tensile stress (y-axis); the points to mark are \(A\) the proportional limit, \(B\) the yield point or elastic limit, \(C\) a point in the plastic region with the unloading line \(CE\) drawn from it to the strain axis, and \(D\) the breaking point; and the straight portion \(OA\) nearest the origin is the region in which Hooke's law is obeyed.

**Given:** \(m = 50\) kg; the object just begins to move when the spring balance reads \(50\) N, so the limiting force of static friction is \(F_L = 50\) N; \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the coefficient of static friction \(\mu_s\).

The table is horizontal, so the normal reaction is

\[ N = mg = 50 \times 9.8 = 490\ \text{N} \]

By the first law of static friction, \(F_L = \mu_s N\), so

\[ \mu_s = \frac{F_L}{N} = \frac{50}{490} = 0.1020 \]

**The coefficient of static friction is \(\mu_s \approx 0.102\)** (a pure number, with no unit).

**Given:** \(m = 37\) kg; \(\mu_s = 0.3\); \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the least force required to just move the block horizontally.

The plane is horizontal, so the normal reaction is

\[ N = mg = 37 \times 9.8 = 362.6\ \text{N} \]

The least force needed to just start the motion is the limiting force of static friction:

\[ F_L = \mu_s N = 0.3 \times 362.6 = 108.78\ \text{N} \]

**The least force required is about \(108.8\) N** (\(1.088 \times 10^{2}\) N).

**Given:** \(m = 37\) kg; force to just start the motion \(F_L = 68.5\) N; force to keep it moving with constant velocity \(F_k = 43\) N; \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).

**To find:** (a) \(\mu_s\) and (b) \(\mu_k\).

The surface is horizontal, so for both parts the normal reaction is

\[ N = mg = 37 \times 9.8 = 362.6\ \text{N} \]

**(a) Coefficient of static friction.** The minimum force that just starts the motion is the limiting force of static friction, so

\[ \mu_s = \frac{F_L}{N} = \frac{68.5}{362.6} = 0.1889 \]

**(b) Coefficient of kinetic friction.** Moving with constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the applied force is balanced exactly by the force of kinetic friction, \(F_k = 43\) N. Hence

\[ \mu_k = \frac{F_k}{N} = \frac{43}{362.6} = 0.1186 \]

**\(\mu_s \approx 0.189\) and \(\mu_k \approx 0.119\)**, and as expected \(\mu_s > \mu_k\) for the same pair of surfaces.

**Given:** first wire, extension \(l_1 = 4\) mm. Second wire: same material (so the same \(Y\)), same load (so the same \(F\)), length \(L_2 = \dfrac{L_1}{2}\), diameter \(D_2 = 2D_1\).

**To find:** the change in length \(l_2\) of the second wire.

From \(Y = \dfrac{FL}{Al}\),

\[ l = \frac{FL}{AY} \]

Since the diameter is doubled, the area \(A = \dfrac{\pi D^{2}}{4}\) becomes four times as large:

\[ A_2 = \frac{\pi (2D_1)^{2}}{4} = 4 \times \frac{\pi D_1^{2}}{4} = 4A_1 \]

With \(F\) and \(Y\) the same for both wires,

\[ \frac{l_2}{l_1} = \frac{L_2}{L_1} \times \frac{A_1}{A_2} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8} \]

\[ \therefore\; l_2 = \frac{l_1}{8} = \frac{4}{8} = 0.5\ \text{mm} \]

**The second wire stretches by \(0.5\) mm**, that is \(5 \times 10^{-4}\) m.

**Given:** \(L = 2\) m; \(A = 0.0225\) mm\(^{2}\) \(= 0.0225 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{2}\) \(= 2.25 \times 10^{-8}\) m\(^{2}\); \(F = 100\) N applied slowly; \(Y = 2 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the work done in stretching the wire.

First find the elongation. From \(Y = \dfrac{FL}{Al}\),

\[ l = \frac{FL}{AY} = \frac{100 \times 2}{\left(2.25 \times 10^{-8}\right)\left(2 \times 10^{11}\right)} = \frac{200}{4500} = 4.444 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{m} \]

The load is applied slowly, so the stretching force grows from zero to \(F\) and the work done is

\[ W = \frac{1}{2}\,(\text{load})\,(\text{extension}) = \frac{1}{2}Fl = \frac{1}{2} \times 100 \times 4.444 \times 10^{-2} \]

\[ W = 2.222\ \text{J} \]

**The work done is about \(2.22\) J**, and this is stored in the wire as strain energy.

[Textbook note: the printed answer gives only the order of magnitude, \(10^{-4}\) m\(^{3}\). The value that follows from the stem is \(1.016 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{3}\), and it is a DECREASE in volume, which the printed answer does not say.]

**Given:** \(V = 0.31\) m\(^{3}\); change in pressure \(dP = 2 \times 10^{7}\) N/m\(^{2}\); \(K = 6.1 \times 10^{10}\) N/m\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the change in volume \(dV\).

The sphere is under volume (hydraulic) stress, so

\[ K = \frac{V\,dP}{dV} \qquad \therefore\; dV = \frac{V\,dP}{K} \]

\[ dV = \frac{0.31 \times 2 \times 10^{7}}{6.1 \times 10^{10}} = \frac{6.2 \times 10^{6}}{6.1 \times 10^{10}} \]

\[ dV = 1.016 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{3} \]

**The change in volume is about \(1.02 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{3}\), and it is a decrease** in volume, since the water pressure compresses the sphere.

**Given:** \(L = 1.5\) m; diameter \(D = 0.60\) mm, so radius \(r = 0.30\) mm \(= 3.0 \times 10^{-4}\) m; \(l = 6.3\) mm \(= 6.3 \times 10^{-3}\) m; \(Y = 2.1 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the force applied.

Area of cross section:

\[ A = \pi r^{2} = 3.142 \times \left(3.0 \times 10^{-4}\right)^{2} = 2.827 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{2} \]

From \(Y = \dfrac{FL}{Al}\),

\[ F = \frac{YAl}{L} = \frac{\left(2.1 \times 10^{11}\right)\left(2.827 \times 10^{-7}\right)\left(6.3 \times 10^{-3}\right)}{1.5} \]

\[ F = \frac{374.1}{1.5} = 249.4\ \text{N} \]

**The force applied is about \(249\) N** (\(2.49 \times 10^{2}\) N).

[Textbook answer-key error, plus an unphysical given. The wires are in series with the same length and cross-section, so each extends in proportion to \(1/Y\); with the values AS PRINTED that gives tungsten \(3.2445\) mm and steel \(0.005516\) mm, which sum to exactly the \(3.25\) mm the question states. The printed key gives the steel extension as \(0.0052\) mm, and its two figures sum to \(3.2492\) mm — they do not reach the total the stem itself supplies, which is what identifies the steel value as the wrong one. Separately, the given \(Y_{\text{Tungsten}} = 3.40 \times 10^{8}\) N/m\(^{2}\) is not tungsten: the real value is about \(3.4 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\), STIFFER than steel, so physically the tungsten wire must extend LESS than the steel one rather than some six hundred times more. It is also forty times below lead, the least stiff metal in this chapter's own Table 6.1. The question is solved as printed; with the physical value the extensions would instead be \(1.204\) mm and \(2.046\) mm.]

**Given:** a tungsten wire and a steel wire of equal length \(L\) and equal cross-sectional area \(A\), joined end to end; total extension \(l_t + l_s = 3.25\) mm; \(Y_{steel} = 2 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\); \(Y_{Tungsten} = 3.40 \times 10^{8}\) N/m\(^{2}\) as printed in the question.

**To find:** the increase in length of each wire separately.

The two wires are joined end to end and the load hangs from the free end, so **the same force \(F\) acts in both wires**. From \(Y = \dfrac{FL}{Al}\),

\[ l = \frac{FL}{AY} \]

With \(F\), \(L\) and \(A\) the same for both, the extension is inversely proportional to Young's modulus:

\[ \frac{l_t}{l_s} = \frac{Y_{steel}}{Y_{Tungsten}} = \frac{2 \times 10^{11}}{3.40 \times 10^{8}} = 588.2 \]

So \(l_t = 588.2\,l_s\). Substituting in \(l_t + l_s = 3.25\) mm,

\[ 588.2\,l_s + l_s = 3.25 \qquad \therefore\; l_s = \frac{3.25}{589.2} = 5.52 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mm} \]

\[ l_t = 3.25 - 0.00552 = 3.244\ \text{mm} \]

**Increase in length of the tungsten wire \(\approx 3.244\) mm (\(3.244 \times 10^{-3}\) m); increase in length of the steel wire \(\approx 5.52 \times 10^{-3}\) mm (\(5.52 \times 10^{-6}\) m).** Practically the whole of the \(3.25\) mm extension is taken up by the tungsten wire.

[Note on the data: the value \(Y_{Tungsten} = 3.40 \times 10^{8}\) N/m\(^{2}\) given in the question is not the value for tungsten. Real tungsten has \(Y \approx 3.4 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\), which is **stiffer** than steel, so the tungsten wire should stretch **less** than the steel wire, not roughly six hundred times more. Compare Table 6.1 of this chapter, where even lead, the least stiff metal listed, has \(Y = 1.5 \times 10^{10}\) N/m\(^{2}\) - about forty times the printed figure. The working above solves the question exactly as printed; with the physical value \(3.4 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\) the answer would instead be \(l_t = 1.204\) mm and \(l_s = 2.046\) mm.]

[Textbook misprint: the stem gives "a lateral strain of \(1.455\) mm", attaching a unit to a dimensionless ratio. Read as \(1.455 \times 10^{-4}\) the printed answer \(0.291\) follows exactly — and that reading is corroborated by this chapter's own Table 6.4, which gives Poisson's ratio for steel as \(0.28\) and puts common metals in the range \(0.25\)–\(0.35\).]

**Given:** \(A = 1.2\) mm\(^{2}\) \(= 1.2 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{2}\); \(F = 120\) N; lateral strain \(= 1.455 \times 10^{-4}\); \(Y_{steel} = 2 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\).

**To find:** Poisson's ratio \(\sigma\).

First find the longitudinal (linear) strain. The longitudinal stress is

\[ \text{stress} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{120}{1.2 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.0 \times 10^{8}\ \text{N/m}^{2} \]

and since \(Y = \dfrac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}\),

\[ \text{linear strain} = \frac{\text{stress}}{Y} = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{8}}{2 \times 10^{11}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4} \]

Poisson's ratio is the ratio of lateral strain to linear strain:

\[ \sigma = \frac{\text{lateral strain}}{\text{linear strain}} = \frac{1.455 \times 10^{-4}}{5.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 0.291 \]

**Poisson's ratio is \(\sigma = 0.291\)**, a pure number with no unit. This is close to the value \(0.28\) given for steel in Table 6.4 of this chapter, and it lies in the range \(0.25\) to \(0.35\) that the chapter quotes for most commonly used metals.

[Note on the data: the question states "a lateral strain of \(1.455\) mm". Strain is a ratio of two similar quantities and is therefore dimensionless, so it cannot carry the unit mm. The figure has been read as the dimensionless lateral strain \(1.455 \times 10^{-4}\), which is the reading that makes the data self-consistent and returns a Poisson's ratio for steel that agrees with the chapter's own Table 6.4.]

**Given:** \(L = 125\) m; \(r = 1\) mm \(= 1 \times 10^{-3}\) m; stretched length \(= 125.25\) m, so \(l = 125.25 - 125 = 0.25\) m; \(F = 800\) N.

**To find:** Young's modulus \(Y\) of the material of the wire.

Area of cross section:

\[ A = \pi r^{2} = 3.142 \times \left(1 \times 10^{-3}\right)^{2} = 3.142 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2} \]

\[ Y = \frac{FL}{Al} = \frac{800 \times 125}{\left(3.142 \times 10^{-6}\right) \times 0.25} \]

\[ Y = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{5}}{7.854 \times 10^{-7}} = 1.273 \times 10^{11}\ \text{N/m}^{2} \]

**Young's modulus of the material is about \(1.27 \times 10^{11}\) N/m\(^{2}\)**, which by Table 6.1 of this chapter is close to the value for copper (\(11.0 \times 10^{10}\) N/m\(^{2}\)).

**Given:** original length \(L = 30\) cm; stretched length \(= 32\) cm, so the change in length is \(\Delta l = 32 - 30 = 2\) cm.

**To find:** the strain produced.

Strain is the ratio of the change in dimension to the original dimension:

\[ \text{strain} = \frac{\Delta l}{L} = \frac{2}{30} = 0.0667 \]

**The strain produced is \(0.0667\)**, that is \(6.67 \times 10^{-2}\). Both lengths are in the same unit, so the units cancel and the strain is a dimensionless number; there is no need to convert the centimetres to metres.

**Given:** \(A = 0.01\) cm\(^{2}\); load \(m = 100\) kg, so \(F = mg = 100 \times 9.8 = 980\) N; \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).

**To find:** the stress in the wire.

Convert the area to SI units. Since \(1\ \text{cm}^{2} = 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^{2}\),

\[ A = 0.01\ \text{cm}^{2} = 0.01 \times 10^{-4} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^{2} \]

\[ \text{stress} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{980}{1 \times 10^{-6}} \]

\[ \text{stress} = 9.8 \times 10^{8}\ \text{N/m}^{2} \]

**The stress in the wire is \(9.8 \times 10^{8}\) N/m\(^{2}\) (Pa).** The length of \(50\) m is not needed: stress depends only on the force and the area of cross section.

**Given:** original length \(L = 50\) m; increase in length \(\Delta l = 2.5\) cm \(= 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\) m.

**To find:** the strain in the cable.

\[ \text{strain} = \frac{\Delta l}{L} = \frac{2.5 \times 10^{-2}}{50} \]

\[ \text{strain} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \]

**The strain in the cable is \(5 \times 10^{-4}\)** (that is \(0.0005\)), a dimensionless number with no unit. Note that the two lengths had to be brought to the same unit before dividing.
